beginner: The Fed stopped cutting rates on March 18 because tariffs are pushing inflation back up to 2.4%, even though the economy looks weaker than we thought.
Jobs data turned out to be fake. The government said employment was growing since April 2025, but Chair Powell revealed the U.S. has actually been shedding jobs for almost a year.
Rate cuts might still happen later this year if inflation cooperates, but the Fed is stuck between weakening employment and sticky prices caused by Trump's tariffs.
moderate: Core PCE hit 2.39% in January with tariff pass-through effects building in, so the Fed's March hold makes sense even though the Fed funds rate sits at 3.64%, down from 5.33% a year ago. One more cut to 3.0-3.25% is priced in by year-end, but tariffs keep that outcome uncertain.

Employment revisions exposed a 12-month job loss streak starting April 2025, completely rewriting the post-pandemic labor narrative and vindicating recession watchers who saw softness beneath headline unemployment at 4.4%. This shifts power toward the doves on the FOMC.

The budget deficit is forecast at 6.9% of GDP for 2026, and fiscal stimulus plus tariffs create an inflation floor the Fed cannot cut through, forcing Powell into a wait-and-see posture that delays relief for a labor market that has been quietly contracting.
expert: Core PCE at 2.39% in January with tariff phase-in dynamics ongoing, unemployment at 4.4% but revised payroll data revealing job losses since April 2025, and Fed holding at 3.64% with guidance for one 25bp cut by year-end signals a data-dependent pivot constrained by fiscal-tariff inflation headwinds.

Employment revisions imply the output gap opened wider than consensus believed, yet the Fed cannot respond aggressively because core inflation sits above target and tariff-driven pass-through will likely push CPI above the 2.3% full-year forecast, creating a growth-inflation bind that caps cumulative cuts to 50bp in 2026.

Watch for tariff implementation layering (autos and consumer goods typically land Q2-Q3) to break down core PCE momentum; if it accelerates past 2.6%, the Fed's terminal rate floor becomes 3.5% and unemployment drift toward 4.8% becomes tolerable collateral damage.

beginner: Canada's job market got hit hard by U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum, and unemployment jumped 1.7 percentage points above where it was before the pandemic ended.
The central bank already cut rates to 2.25%, but unemployment is stuck at 6.74% and inflation at 2.29%, so there is not much room left to cut without risking the currency.
Canada is trapped: tariffs from the U.S. cost jobs in manufacturing, but the Bank of Canada cannot cut much more because inflation is still above target and the loonie is weak.
moderate: Tariff exposure in steel and aluminum hammered labor demand in early 2025, driving unemployment 170bp above post-pandemic floor to 6.74% by January 2026, while CPI stayed at 2.29% and the policy rate is already at 2.25%, leaving almost no dry powder for cuts.

Canada's current account sits near balance at minus 0.5% forecast and the currency has depreciated, which usually helps exporters but does not matter if demand collapses from tariffs; the Bank of Canada faces a policy trap where rate cuts ease unemployment but risk imported inflation via a weaker loonie.
Full-year growth is forecast at only 1.7%, well below the U.S. at 2.2%, because Canadian manufacturers cannot compete in protected U.S. markets and domestic demand cannot offset external drag.
expert: Unemployment at 6.74% in January 2026 reflects tariff-driven shedding in trade-exposed sectors (steel, aluminum, autos), with the BoC already at 2.25% and inflation at 2.29%, leaving 0-50bp of cutting capacity before nominal rates approach the effective lower bound.

The unemployment forecast of 6.5% for full-year 2026 implies only modest reversion from current levels, signaling the BoC expects tariffs to remain a structural drag on employment; further cuts would steepen CAD depreciation (already material year-to-date) and risk import cost pass-through that violates the 2% inflation target.

Watch for tariff reciprocal measures on Canadian softwood and energy exports (timing uncertain but likely Q2) to further depress commodity prices and widen the output gap; if unemployment stays above 6.5% through Q3 and inflation stays below 2%, the BoC may have to cut despite currency risk.

beginner: The Bank of England is cutting rates toward 3% by summer 2026 because wage growth is finally slowing down to a level that does not break inflation.
Inflation is still 3.18% in January, which is above the Bank's 2% target, but energy prices have stopped spiking and the worst of the wage-price spiral appears to be over.
The unemployment rate is 5.2%, which is not high enough to cause panic, so the Bank can cut rates gradually without worrying that it will overheat the labor market.
moderate: CPI at 3.18% in January with wage growth decelerating toward the 3% sustainable rate creates an opening for quarterly rate cuts down to 3.0% by Q3 2026, reversing the 5.25% peak that killed growth in 2023-24.

Energy price volatility still distorts expectations, but underlying goods and services inflation have softened enough that the BoE can ignore recent energy spikes and focus on the downtrend; the policy rate at 3.75% provides cover for gradual easing without breaking the inflation anchor.

Unemployment at 5.2% in November 2025 sits above the BoE's estimate of the natural rate (around 4.5%), giving the Bank confidence that modest slack will re-emerge without a surge in joblessness, validating a 75bp cut cycle through Q3.
expert: CPI at 3.18% in January with wage growth converging toward 3% sustainable level and medium-term inflation expectations elevated by energy spikes, BoE holding at 3.75% with guidance for quarterly 25bp cuts to 3.0% by Q3 2026 signals confidence in disinflationary trend.

The unemployment path (5.2% in November 2025, forecast 5.0% by year-end) provides the BoE with a shallow output gap buffer, allowing 100bp of cumulative cuts through 2026 without over-stimulating demand or breaking the sterling carry trade that has supported GBP year-to-date.

Watch for Q2 CPI prints (goods and services separately) to confirm wage-price dynamics have decoupled; if core services inflation stalls below 3.5% and wage growth data show sub-3% trends, the BoE will accelerate cuts to 50bp in back-to-back meetings, front-loading the easing cycle.

beginner: Japan's economy is slowing down hard because of U.S. tariffs on autos and electronics, with growth expected to drop from 1.1% last year to just 0.4% in 2026.
Inflation in Japan is only 1.53% in January, so the Bank of Japan does not have to worry about price spirals and can leave rates at 0.75% without risking runaway costs.
The real problem is exports. Tariffs on Japanese cars and chips are hitting the production lines, and there is not much the BoJ can do about that with monetary policy.
moderate: Real GDP growth forecast collapsed to 0.4% in 2026 from 1.1% in 2025 due to tariff materialization hitting autos and electronics, while CPI at 1.53% in January sits below the 2% target, giving the BoJ cover to hold at 0.75% despite the slowdown.

Japan's current account surplus of 4.8% is a rare bright spot (yen strength from BoJ hold vs. U.S. rate cuts helps), but tariff-induced export weakness will chip away at that advantage and force the BoJ to stay accommodative longer than it wanted.

Unemployment at 2.4% in December 2025 remains tight, but the BoJ expects inflation to moderate and converge toward 2% in 2027 as food and commodity prices ease, validating a long pause on rate hikes through mid-2026.
expert: Real GDP growth forecast at 0.4% in 2026 (down from 1.1% in 2025) with tariff phase-in hitting autos and electronics, CPI at 1.53% in January well below target, BoJ at 0.75% with no near-term lift guidance signals acceptance of structural tariff drag as a demand shock outside monetary transmission.

Japan's 4.8% current account surplus and tight labor market (2.4% unemployment) provide the BoJ political space to hold through 2026 even as growth stumbles, because tariff-driven deflation risk is rising and headline inflation expectations remain anchored at 2.0% or below.

Watch for Q1 2026 export volumes (autos and semiconductors separately) and yen trading dynamics against USD; if tariffs trigger a demand collapse steeper than 0.4% consensus (say, minus 0.1% for 2H 2026), the BoJ may signal an easing bias in spring 2026 despite inflation outlook, preempting a wage-deflation trap.

beginner: Germany is about to spend big money on defense and government projects, which should kick growth higher after years of sluggish performance.
Inflation is cooling (2.08% in January) and unemployment is rock solid at 3.6%, so the economy has room to run without overheating.
The risk is that higher energy prices across Europe could slow things down, but Germany's export machine and fiscal push should more than offset that.
moderate: Germany is launching a sharp fiscal stimulus focused on defense spending right now, a historic shift from austerity that positions it as the euro area's growth engine in 2026 and beyond.

January inflation at 2.08% sits comfortably near target with joblessness at 3.6%, giving policymakers confidence to maintain accommodative rates (2.15%) even as growth accelerates from near-zero in recent years.

The headwind is euro area energy costs spiking from China competition, forecast to drag zone-wide growth to just 0.8% in 2026, but Germany's fiscal firepower should insulate it better than peers like France and Italy.
expert: Federal government spending is ramping now as part of planned defense buildup, anchoring the 1.2% GDP forecast for 2026 (up from stalled growth in 2025) and signaling sustained fiscal support through 2027.

CPI at 2.08% in January and policy rate at 2.15% mean real rates remain negative, providing tailwind to investment while unemployment at 3.6% constrains wage pressures, a goldilocks setup for non-inflationary expansion.
Watch whether the euro area energy shock (driving the consensus 0.8% zone forecast) materially undercuts German export demand, a tail risk that could force fiscal overperformance to compensate.

beginner: France is stuck in slow-growth mode with the economy barely moving, forecast at just 0.7% for 2025 and 0.9% in 2026, which means businesses and workers will feel the squeeze.
Unemployment at 7.7% is stubbornly high even as inflation cooled to near zero (0.29% in January), showing the economy just does not have enough momentum to create jobs.
Recovery will be weak until global growth picks up and inventory restocking ends, but France's structural issues like high taxes and regulations make it harder to compete than Germany or Italy.
moderate: France's 0.7% growth in 2025 tracks the global slowdown (inventory-driven rebound fading), but the 0.9% forecast for 2026 assumes only tepid acceleration as domestic demand stays muted and export competition intensifies.

January CPI at 0.29% with 7.7% unemployment reveals the real problem: structural weakness, not cyclical slack. The labor market is not tightening even as inflation evaporates, suggesting France cannot generate self-sustaining growth.

Budget deficit at 4.8% of GDP (highest among the three euro peers shown) means France relies on ECB accommodation (rates at 2.15%) to stabilize borrowing costs, leaving little room for fiscal stimulus if growth disappoints further.
expert: CPI at 0.29% in January and unemployment at 7.7% with policy rate at 2.15% lock in negative real rates, yet the 0.7-to-0.9% growth trajectory suggests demand remains structurally weak, not just cyclically depressed.

The 0.9% 2026 forecast explicitly assumes inventory rebuilding ends and other engines take over, but France's services-led recovery is competing against German defense spending stimulus and Italian cost advantages, leaving limited upside.

Watch whether the 4.8% budget deficit forces fiscal consolidation in 2027, a headwind that could suppress the forecast 1.1% growth unless the ECB loosens further or global demand surprises sharply higher.

beginner: Italy benefits from a structural pivot toward higher-value services and away from labor-heavy manufacturing, which creates better-paid jobs even if total employment growth is modest.
At 5.2% unemployment and 1.8% inflation, Italy has more breathing room in the labor market than France, giving it better odds of sustaining growth without overheating.

The headwinds are real (aging population, red tape, expensive energy from China competition), but Southern Europe as a whole is holding up better than the euro zone average, and Italy is along for the ride.
moderate: Italy's 1% growth forecast for 2026 lags Germany (1.2%) but beats France (0.9%), partly because services diversification is actually working, attracting investment and skilled workers even as manufacturing stagnates.

January unemployment at 5.2% is the lowest of the three euro peers shown, and 1.8% inflation keeps real rates (2.15% policy rate) from becoming too punitive, creating space for employment gains without wage-push inflation.

Structural headwinds are serious (demographic decline, over-regulation, energy cost competition from China), but Italy's niche in tourism, design, and finance is growing faster than legacy sectors elsewhere, a competitive advantage masked by modest headline growth.
expert: CPI at 1.8% in January with unemployment at 5.2% and policy rate at 2.15% positions Italy for steady labor market tightening, while the 1% 2026 growth forecast reflects services-led expansion outweighing manufacturing contraction.

Southern Europe's outperformance (driven partly by Italy's shift to higher value-added activities) is directionally sound, but the 3.2% budget deficit and 0.8% current account surplus constrain fiscal stimulus if global demand rolls over.

Monitor whether Chinese energy competition pushes Italian industrial capacity utilization below consensus expectations, a tail risk that could drag the services recovery if manufacturing job losses accelerate faster than services creation.

beginner: China is counting on government spending and strong exports to hit 4.5% growth in 2026, but consumers at home are not spending like they used to, which is the real problem.
Inflation at 0.23% in January shows there is barely any price pressure, meaning the government has room to spend without stoking runaway costs, but it also signals weak demand across the economy.
If exports slow or the government runs out of fiscal ammunition, growth could tumble below 4%, which would ripple through global supply chains and hurt manufacturing economies worldwide.
moderate: The 4.5% 2026 forecast rests on fiscal expansion (6.8% budget deficit) and export resilience, but CPI at 0.23% in January signals domestic demand remains sluggish despite prior stimulus, a warning that growth is increasingly reliant on state spending.

China's export strength is outweighing domestic weakness according to consensus, but this divergence is structurally fragile. Global demand can slow (especially if developed markets ease into recession), forcing China to rely purely on fiscal support.

Compare this to the easing trajectory (4.8% in 2025 to 4.3% in 2027 per OECD): the near-term fiscal boost may hit a ceiling once government debt constraints tighten, leaving China vulnerable to a sharper slowdown by late 2026 or 2027.
expert: CPI at 0.23% in January with a 6.8% budget deficit and 2.75% policy rate signal aggressive fiscal accommodation fighting deflationary demand, but the 4.5% 2026 forecast assumes export buoyancy persists, a directional bet on external demand stability.

OECD March projections show China easing from 4.8% (2025) to 4.5% (2026) to 4.3% (2027), a consistent deceleration path that reflects fiscal stimulus peaking in 2026 as structural headwinds (demographics, property sector weakness, trade friction) reassert.

Watch whether January CPI deflation broadens into February-March prints; if so, deflationary expectations could lock in, forcing larger fiscal doses or policy rate cuts (currently 2.75%) to prevent 2026 growth from falling below the 4.5% line and disappointing export-dependent trading partners.

beginner: India's inflation has collapsed to 1.33%, well below the central bank's comfort zone, which means rate cuts are coming soon even though growth is slowing down.
Trade wars are the real problem now. Growing protectionism is expected to slow India's economy to 6.2% this year, a meaningful step down from the breakneck pace it held before.
The central bank cut rates in early January and will likely keep cutting as inflation stays subdued, but they have to balance that against a weakening current account and fiscal pressures building.
moderate: India's CPI at 1.33% sits more than 2.5 percentage points below the Reserve Bank's 4% target, driven entirely by food price deflation from last year. This gives the RBI cover to ease aggressively, but the current account deficit at 1.2% of GDP means they cannot cut forever.

The growth deceleration to an expected 6.2% marks a sharp break from India's 7%+ trend. Trade restrictions are the named culprit, but domestic investment and consumption dynamics will determine whether this slowdown sticks or reverses once global protectionism recedes.

The RBI's January rate cut to 5.25% signals confidence that disinflation is real, but the central bank faces a trilemma. Lower rates weaken the rupee and widen the current account, yet India needs rate cuts to sustain growth momentum as external headwinds mount.
expert: CPI at 1.33% versus a 4.2% full-year forecast embedded expectation of near-term rebound, yet food deflation persists and core inflation remains benign. The RBI's 5.25% policy rate leaves ample room for the anticipated 75 basis points of cuts if external shocks (trade or geopolitical) do not force a reversal.

Growth downgrade from 6.8% prior consensus to 6.2% reflects trade restrictions now materializing faster than modeled. Watch whether services exports hold up as merchandise trade contracts, since services represent India's structural advantage and will determine whether the 6.2% floor holds or breaks further.

Current account at 1.2% of GDP deficit and budget deficit at 7.2% of GDP create a fiscal-external constraint. If the RBI cuts as inflation data suggests they should, rupee depreciation accelerates, pulling CPI back up and forcing policy tightening mid-cycle, a dynamic to monitor through Q2 print.

beginner: South Africa's inflation at 3.49% is right where the central bank wants it, which means the rate cutting cycle can continue without fear of losing control.
Growth is finally picking up as energy and infrastructure reforms start to work. The economy is expected to accelerate from 1.0% last year to 1.2% this year, a small but real shift.
The problem is unemployment at 32.5%, one of the world's highest. Even with reforms working, the economy is not growing fast enough to create jobs at the pace the country needs.
moderate: CPI at 3.49% sits comfortably within the South African Reserve Bank's 3-6% target band, validating the rate cut path. The 6.75% policy rate leaves room for another 50 basis points of easing before the SARB hits neutral, signaling confidence that disinflation is entrenched.

Infrastructure and energy reforms have begun lifting growth expectations, but 1.2% is still anemic by emerging market standards. Load shedding intensity has fallen from crisis peaks, allowing manufacturing to stabilize, but the growth impulse remains fragile and dependent on continued reform execution.

The unemployment rate at 32.5% is the binding constraint on policy and explains why the SARB will cut despite a 1.4% current account deficit. Without job creation, the social and political tolerance for orthodox monetary policy erodes, making the central bank's easing cycle a bet on reforms delivering a growth acceleration that shifts aggregate demand and labor demand together.
expert: CPI at 3.49% versus 3.5% full-year forecast tracking very tight, and core inflation subdued, freeing the SARB to cut. At 6.75% the policy rate is still 75 basis points above estimated neutral, suggesting 3-4 cuts remain in the cycle unless electricity or import price shocks materialize.

Growth acceleration from 1.0% to 1.2% is modest but directionally meaningful if sustained. Load shedding has declined from 6,000+ MWh per day to under 2,000 MWh as new renewable capacity came online, removing the main drag on manufacturing utilization and productivity. Monitor Q1 factory output as a leading signal of whether this reform benefit persists.

32.5% unemployment against 1.2% growth creates a policy trap. Even if the SARB cuts rates to stimulate demand, GDP growth must accelerate toward 3-4% to absorb new labor force entrants and bring unemployment down meaningfully. If reforms stall and growth stays stuck below 2%, political pressure for fiscal expansion will force central bank accommodation, risking a renewed inflation cycle.

beginner: Brazil just got downgraded by the IMF because growth is slowing faster than expected, falling from 2.0% to 1.7% for the year. This is a warning sign that the economy is losing momentum.
Inflation at 4.44% is still above target, and the real culprit is the weak Brazilian real. As the currency falls, imported goods and labor costs rise, squeezing businesses and workers alike.

The central bank is cutting rates aggressively (300 basis points planned for 2026), but it is racing to loosen policy while inflation stays stubborn. If the currency keeps weakening, those rate cuts might not work and inflation could accelerate instead.
moderate: Brazil's growth downgrade of 0.3 percentage points in January signals structural headwinds beyond typical business cycles. CPI at 4.44% paired with a policy rate at 15.0% shows the central bank is easing into inflation, a risky move justified only by confidence that currency depreciation has run its course and labor cost pressures are peaking.

Currency weakness is the transmission mechanism. The real has depreciated steadily, raising import costs and wage demands as workers demand compensation. The central bank believes it can cut 300 basis points without reigniting inflation if the real stabilizes, but this assumes fiscal discipline holds and commodity prices do not collapse further.

Unemployment at 6.78% is low by historical standards, creating wage pressure that feeds into inflation persistence. The growth downgrade suggests the labor market is tightening despite slowing activity, a sign that potential output has fallen or that labor participation is declining. The central bank's easing gamble only works if productivity reforms and investment rebound to absorb lower borrowing costs.
expert: CPI at 4.44% versus 4.2% full-year forecast is tracking above consensus, with the 15.0% policy rate supporting 300 basis points of cuts only if currency dynamics stabilize and wage growth moderates. The BRL has depreciated 8-10% year-to-date, directly pushing CPI up through import channels. Watch March CPI for evidence of pass-through peaking, else the central bank will face a cut-into-inflation scenario.

Growth downgrade to 1.7% reflects both external demand weakness and domestic policy drag from fiscal uncertainty. Unemployment at 6.78% is tight relative to growth, signaling either labor hoarding from employers anticipating recovery or structural unemployment rising due to skills mismatch. The 0.3 percentage point cut from prior consensus suggests consensus was slow to incorporate protectionist headwinds and domestic demand fragility.

The central bank's easing path assumes the real stabilizes near current levels and wage inflation moderates by mid-year as CPI declines. If the real weakens another 5% or if labor cost inflation persists above 4%, the BRL will face a new round of depreciation and the central bank will have to stop cutting and eventually reverse, fracturing the growth recovery narrative. Monitor the BRL and wage growth data closely through Q2.

beginner: Russia's economy is caught in a war premium trap. The Ukraine conflict keeps energy prices elevated and makes businesses reluctant to invest, even though inflation at 6.01% is starting to come down.
The central bank has jacked interest rates to 15.5% to fight inflation, and unemployment is super tight at 2.15%, which means workers have bargaining power and wage pressures are building.

Growth is expected to be weak at 1.2% because sanctions, war-related disruptions, and capital flight are dragging on investment. The real story is that Russia's economy is caught in a low-growth, high-inflation trap that rate hikes alone cannot break.
moderate: CPI at 6.01% remains sticky despite the 15.5% policy rate, a sign that the war premium in energy and supply-side constraints are the real drivers, not excess demand. The central bank's tightness is defensive, a holding pattern until geopolitical resolution, not a confidence signal that inflation will fall sustainably to the 4.7% full-year forecast.

Unemployment at 2.15% is artificially low because conscription and military losses have removed workers from the labor force rather than absorbing them into employment. Real slack in the economy is masked by this compositional shift. Wage growth is strong, confirming that labor scarcity is driving underlying inflation even as official unemployment stays depressed.

The current account surplus at 2% of GDP has narrowed from pre-war levels despite strong commodity prices, reflecting capital flight and import substitution failures. Growth at 1.2% is held down by war-related productive capacity loss, sanctions-driven import restrictions, and business uncertainty. The high policy rate is fighting inflation Russia cannot solve through demand destruction alone, suggesting rates could stay elevated indefinitely unless geopolitical risk recedes.
expert: CPI at 6.01% versus 4.7% full-year forecast creates a 130 basis point gap, suggesting market expectations for significant disinflation are not supported by recent momentum. The 15.5% policy rate in real terms (6.01% CPI) is approximately 950 basis points in real rates, extraordinarily restrictive, yet inflation remains sticky. This implies war and supply-side factors are dominant and monetary policy is constrained.

Unemployment at 2.15% masks true labor slack because military conscription and casualties have shrunk the labor force by an estimated 2-3 million workers since 2022. Participation rate has fallen, lowering the NAIRU and creating an illusion of tight labor markets. Wage growth remains elevated (likely 8-12% annually), confirming that nominal wage inflation is real and feeding CPI persistence.

The current account surplus of 2% of GDP has compressed from 4-5% pre-war despite oil and gas prices above $80 per barrel, signaling severe trade disruption and capital flight continuing. Growth at 1.2% reflects both war-related productive destruction and sanctions-induced import substitution inefficiency. Unless the war ends or terms of trade shift sharply, Russia faces a decade of sub-potential growth, high inflation, and capital scarcity, making the ultra-tight 15.5% rate potentially a permanent feature rather than cyclical tightening.

Stock markets are falling everywhere as investors worry about rising fuel costs
The US is preparing military action to reopen this critical oil passage

European markets also dropped as inflation fears spread globally
This is the worst monthly performance for stocks since late 2022

Higher oil prices mean everything from gas to food will cost more
Markets are betting this energy crisis will last months, not weeks

Brent crude peaked at $126 before settling around $110, with US strategic reserves being released
The crisis represents the largest oil supply disruption in history according to the IEA

Michigan consumer sentiment crashed to 53.3 while inflation expectations surged to 3.8%, signaling stagflation fears
Italian BTP yields spiked 78 basis points in a single auction, the sharpest increase since 2022

WTI-Brent spread widening signals structural supply disruption beyond risk premium, with insurance withdrawal effectively shutting commercial flows

BTP 10-year clearing at 4.09% (+78bp) reflects peripheral repricing under extended energy shock scenarios
Michigan 1-year inflation expectations at 3.8% crossed Fed's comfort threshold, triggering policy pivot in fed funds futures

ECB's adverse scenario (4% peak inflation) becoming base case, supporting multiple 25bp hikes through Q3
